- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

# Long Term Vision + Goal

This project explores the most efficient ways to run a variety of AI/LLM generations on **Vulkan** using the AMD AI MAX+ 395 "Strix Halo" platform, with gfx1151 and RDNA3.5. 

Ultimately we want to be able to run these tasks:
  1. Speech to Text via Nvidia's `parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3`:
    * https://huggingface.co/nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3
    * https://arxiv.org/html/2509.14128v2
  2. Text generation via Qwen's `Qwen3.8-Next-Flash`:
    * https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
    * https://arxiv.org/html/2608.30320v1
    * We'll need to quantise the weights once we've determined the most efficient method for the hardware
  3. Text to Speech via Hexgrad's `kokoro-82M`:
    * https://huggingface.co/hexgrad/Kokoro-82M
    * https://arxiv.org/html/2306.07691v2
  4. Image generation via Tongyi's `z-image-turbo`:
    * https://huggingface.co/Tongyi-MAI/Z-Image-Turbo
    * https://arxiv.org/html/2511.22699v5
    * With this smaller model to generate in-progress previews: 
      * https://huggingface.co/madebyollin/taef1
  5. Compute embeddings via Qwen's `Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B`:
    * https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B
    * https://arxiv.org/html/2506.05176v3

We will ultimately serve up a HTTP API serving these features, in Go.

1	# strix-halo-vulkan
2	
3	A Go + Vulkan compute harness for exploring shaders on the Strix Halo iGPU
4	(gfx1151 / AMD Radeon 8060S, RADV driver), plus a benchmark suite
5	(`cmd/bench`) that measures the operations neural-network inference is
6	built from — GEMM, GEMV, elementwise/activation, softmax/RMSNorm — across
7	the implementation "flavours" that matter on this hardware: naive vs.
8	shared-memory-tiled vs. subgroup-reduced vs. cooperative-matrix
9	(`VK_KHR_cooperative_matrix`, RDNA3.5's matrix-multiply accelerator), and
10	fp32 vs. fp16 vs. quantized (int8/int4, GGML-style block scales) weights vs.
11	W8A8 and W4A8 (int8 or 4-bit weights against int8 activations, reduced via
12	`VK_KHR_shader_integer_dot_product`'s packed-dot instructions).
13	
14	Two kernels here are the current answers for the two shapes inference comes
15	in. For **decode** (GEMV, memory-bound), **W4A8**
16	(`shaders/gemv_w4a8.comp`): 4-bit weights fed to the packed-int8 dot
17	instruction through its mixed-signedness overload, at **239 GB/s against
18	DRAM-resident weights — 101% of this machine's 236 GB/s measured memory
19	bandwidth**, 2.4x the int8-weight kernel it replaces. The last 13% of that is
20	one compile-time constant. Size the load width so that a single lane-step
21	covers a whole weight row — `VEC = N/(8·WAVE)`, i.e. `uvec4` at N=2048, two
22	at N=4096, four at N=8192 for a wave64 pipeline — and the kernel reads
23	**99-103% of the bus at every one of those N**: 243, 239 and 235 GB/s. Get it
24	wrong and it does not: the same kernel at one `uvec4` reads 164 GB/s at
25	N=8192, 70% of the bus. This is the `stride` family's coverage law (below)
26	applied from inside a kernel, with the weight row as the stride, and it is
27	what an earlier reading of the same data mistook for a **wave32** effect —
28	holding the bytes-per-lane-step fixed and varying the wave size instead
29	measures the same bandwidth to 0.05%, so the wave32 pin that used to be
30	recommended here is withdrawn (IDEAS §1.7). For **prefill** (GEMM,
31	compute-bound), the register-blocked cooperative-matrix GEMM
32	(`shaders/gemm_wmma.comp`): **39.0 TFLOP/s, 70% of this chip's measured
33	55.5 TFLOP/s of matrix-core throughput** (30.6 TFLOP/s at N=4096), 7.6x the
34	straightforward coopmat kernel it replaces at that shape. Two thirds of that
35	came from neither tiling nor instruction selection but from how the operands
36	meet the memory system. First *stride*: every fragment load in a WMMA GEMM is
37	K-strided, a power-of-two leading dimension aims all the addresses of one
38	load at the same memory channel, and padding each stride 256 B off a 4 KB
39	multiple — a host-side allocation change — is worth up to 1.35x on the
40	kernels that were already winning and 2.6x on the [N,K] weight layout. Then
41	*concurrency*: issuing a whole K-slab's fragment loads before the slab's
42	first MMA, rather than one K-tile's worth at a time, is worth a further
43	**2.1x** for identical bytes, identical instruction counts and an identical
44	tile — only the scheduling moves, from 16 loads in flight to 45. The same
45	slab depth *without* that change leaves 16 in flight and is worth nothing,
46	which is what says the variable is concurrency rather than depth. Together
47	they make the [N,K] layout a real `Linear` weight already has the fastest
48	one, where it used to be 2.8x the slowest.
49	
50	The `stride` family then measured that memory system directly
51	(`shaders/strided_read.comp`) and found a second, larger effect with no
52	kernel-side cause at all: channel interleave on this part is 256 B across
53	sixteen channels, so a row shorter than `gcd(stride, 4096)` bytes **never
54	addresses some of them**, and the achievable fraction of DRAM bandwidth is
55	exactly `min(1, rowBytes/gcd(stride, 4096))`. A K=1024 fp16 weight matrix
56	whose rows were aligned to 4 KB reads at **half** this chip's bandwidth; 1 KB
57	rows at an 8 KB stride, a **quarter** — and unlike the aliasing above this
58	hits a plainly contiguous read as hard as a gather.
59	
60	Swapping the probe's traversal so consecutive *waves* start on consecutive
61	rows — the same bytes, the same instructions, the same checksum — then
62	generalised that into one law about concurrency: the achievable
63	fraction of peak is `min(1, C/gcd(stride, 4096))` where **C is the
64	contiguous run of bytes the requests in flight at one moment hold in a
65	row**, which is the whole row only when consecutive waves walk along it. A
66	*densely* packed tensor is not safe after all: 1 KB rows packed at a 1 KB
67	stride, read with 256 B of each row in flight, run at **61 of 243 GB/s**,
68	with no padding anywhere to blame. One wave streaming a *whole* row
69	— the GEMV kernels' shape — is clean at every stride, and 4 KB of a row in
70	flight per wave restores full bandwidth whatever the stride is. What is
71	exposed is tiling: a 1 KB-wide panel of a K=4096 fp16 matrix gets a quarter
72	of the bus. Pad every row stride to 256 B past a multiple of 4 KB and all
73	three effects go away, for every panel width and every traversal — and where
74	the stride is not the engine's to choose, depth in the inner loop buys the
75	same thing, which is the 2.1x the GEMM above collects. `IDEAS.md`
76	explains how each kernel gets where it is and what is still on the table.
77	
78	All of the above was measured on square N x N x N, which no transformer layer
79	is. The `shapes` family runs the same kernels over the actual (M,N,K) triples
80	of the models in `GOALS.md` — read out of their own configs — and two of the
81	answers change. **Decode gets easier**: every reduction length those models
82	use is a non-power-of-two, so its 4-bit weight row has a *smaller* `gcd` with
83	the 4 KB channel rotation than the square sweep's rows did, and the load width
84	stops mattering. At K=2560, the width every Qwen projection reduces over, the
85	kernel reads 239-242 GB/s at *all four* built widths including the narrowest
86	— where at the square sweep's N=8192 only the widest got there. Only K=1024
87	still needs a `uvec4` (211 → 239 GB/s), and nothing in any of the five models
88	needs a load wider than the kernel already has. **Prefill gets a second
89	kernel**: the suite's headline GEMM wins every shape with 1024 or more tokens
90	in the batch and *loses every shape below that*, by up to 2.8x, to the
91	small-tile wave32 variant the square sweep only ever crowned at N=1024. Real
92	batches are below it constantly — 128 caption tokens, 384 audio frames, and
93	40 tokens per expert when a 2048-token prompt is routed across 512 of them.
94	The crossover is in M alone, and a sweep with M tied to N and K cannot see
95	it.
96	
97	The one shape none of that covers is the **MoE** FFN: qwen3.8-flash-next
98	routes each token to 10 of 512 experts, so its feed-forward block is 512
99	GEMMs over 40-row groups rather than one GEMM, and at prefill it is 1440 of
100	the 1861 matmuls a token costs. The `moe` family builds it — the same WMMA
101	kernel with its tile origin read out of a table instead of derived from
102	`gl_WorkGroupID`, so one dispatch covers every expert — and measures it
103	against the expert-at-a-time loop it replaces, plus the gather and combine
104	passes it makes necessary. Three answers, none of which was the expected one.
105	**Grouping is worth 1.1-4.1x, and it is an occupancy effect, not a launch
106	one**: sort the cells by how many workgroups one expert's dispatch launches
107	and the speedup falls monotonically from 4.1x at 10 workgroups to ~1.1x at
108	80, which is exactly the two-waves-per-CU this part needs to issue WMMA at
109	rate — the 300 ns launch itself is nothing against a 20 µs dispatch. **Tile
110	padding is real and costs nothing**: a 16-row tile takes an expert's group
111	from 62% useful to 84%, and is *slower*, because at these shapes the binding
112	constraint is weight bytes and a smaller tile reads more of them. The grouped
113	kernel moves 190 GB/s of a 236 GB/s bus at the real prefill shape, so there is
114	no room for the FLOPs to matter. And **the "pad every stride by 256 B" rule
115	this suite has been carrying is the wrong statement of itself**: sweeping
116	`gcd(row stride, 4096)` over every power of two at two non-power-of-two
117	reduction lengths gives a plateau at 128-256 B and a cliff on both sides, so
118	what matters is landing the gcd at 128-256 B — which the 640-wide down
119	projection already does unpadded, and which padding it by 256 B *breaks*, for
120	1.19x.
121	
122	That left MoE prefill with exactly one lever — it was at 93% of the ceiling
123	its *format* implies, and that ceiling is 5.03 GB of fp16 expert weights per
124	block. Holding the same kernel and the same schedule and putting the bank at
125	**4 bits** (`shaders/gemm_wmma_q4.comp`) takes one MoE block from 28.13 ms to
126	**13.37 ms** and a 48-layer prompt chunk from 1.35 s to **0.64 s**. Removing
127	4x of the bytes buys 2.1x of the time, and the gap is the finding: the phase
128	stops being a memory problem partway through the change. Weight traffic goes
129	from 190 GB/s of a 236 GB/s bus to 113, while the padded tiles' own rate goes
130	from 22% of the matrix cores to **51%** — half of each ceiling, pinned
131	against neither, with the dequant loop body left as what binds.
132	
133	Three things that cost more than the arithmetic did. **The operand has to
134	round-trip through LDS**, because no cooperative-matrix extension exposes a
135	fragment's lane layout — `m[i]` is defined, which (row, col) it means is not
136	— so 4-bit weights cannot be unpacked into registers and declared a fragment.
137	**That LDS tile's rows must be padded off the 32-bank rotation**: a slab row
138	is 128 B, exactly one rotation, so a 16-row fragment load hits one bank
139	sixteen times, and eight halves of pad are worth **1.68-1.83x** for 28 bytes
140	of code. And **the quantization block size is worth 1.24x between two
141	binaries that are instruction-for-instruction identical** — same VGPRs, same
142	code size, same VALU and VMEM counts, 4.4% of nominal bytes standing behind a
143	24% difference — which is still unattributed. Two predictions did come true:
144	the 16-row tile that *lost* at fp16 because padding cost FLOPs and FLOPs were
145	free now wins, and grouping is worth *more* than it was (5-8x at ten
146	workgroups per expert dispatch, against fp16's 3-4x), because the idle time
147	an under-filled dispatch leaves is fixed and a faster kernel makes it a bigger
148	share. One rule got amended instead: **the stride window above stops paying
149	once a kernel is not bandwidth-bound**, since padding into it still costs
150	bytes — on the down projection, climbing from its natural gcd of 64 into the
151	128-256 B plateau costs 1.20-2.40x the traffic and measures slower.
152	
153	All of that is prefill. **Decode** on the same block was, until now, measured
154	with that same grouped GEMM run at one row per expert — 15 of every 16 rows of
155	each cooperative-matrix tile being padding, and the 8 MB an expert slice
156	occupies sitting inside the 32 MiB MALL, so the timing loop re-read it out of
157	cache. The honest kernel is the W4A8 GEMV with the same table
158	(`shaders/gemv_w4a8.comp -DGROUPED=1`): one subgroup per output row, one
159	workgroup per (row, routed pair), and **no gather pass at all**, since the
160	gather exists only to make an expert's rows consecutive for a fragment load
161	and a subgroup reads whichever row the table names. It is **1.3-3.3x the GEMM
162	at M=1** — same weight bytes, but 2-6 GB/s of activation traffic against 17-41
163	and no 7-11%-useful tiles — reads **235 GB/s of distinct weight bytes, 100% of
164	the bus**, and takes one token's MoE FFN from 9.56 ms to **5.47 ms across 48
165	layers (183 tok/s), 91% of the 5.00 ms its 1.18 GB of 4-bit weights cost at the
166	bus**. Three things fell out of it. **Grouping is worth 1.29-1.81x even though
167	every dispatch it merges already fills the machine**, because what a barrier
168	costs a memory-bound dispatch is the *drain* — 1163 ns median, against the
169	300 ns an empty shader's launch measures. **The crossover back to the GEMM is
170	at about 1.2 rows per expert**, not at the 16 a tile holds, because the
171	question is how many rows of *one* expert routing supplies. And, reversing the
172	rule above once more, **an expert bank should not be padded at all**: with
173	every stride 64 B-aligned so the pad is never read, the unpadded stride wins at
174	both projections — including the down projection's gcd-64 row, which the
175	plateau says should be the slow end — and padding into the window costs
176	1.12-1.15x. The plateau is a property of a *tiled* read, where a fragment holds
177	32 B of a row; a kernel that walks whole matrices just wants them contiguous.
178	
179	That 1.2-rows-per-expert crossover is the one thing a serving engine cannot
180	live with, so the same kernel took an **M block** (`-DMROWS=n`): a workgroup
181	loads an expert's weight row once and dots it against *n* routed tokens, each
182	with its own accumulator and output row, with short groups padded out to keep
183	the inner loop branchless. At 256 sequences in flight — 5.05 rows per expert —
184	it is worth **1.39-1.66x**, and it takes the FFN to **694 tok/s against the
185	GEMM's 546**.
186	At *one* row per expert it is worth **0.39x**, which is the other half of the
187	result: the block has to be picked from the routing, not compiled in once, and
188	the rule is arithmetic — a fitted cost model puts one group (an expert's
189	845 KB through all its output rows) at **6.5-10.5x one slot**, so blocking
190	pays as soon as it removes one group per 6-10 pads it creates, i.e. `MROWS` ≈
191	the mean rows per expert. What the block actually takes off is **not the bus
192	but the cache**: unblocked at five rows per expert the kernel asks for
193	**746 GB/s**, 3.2x the bus, while DRAM underneath it runs at 148 — four fifths
194	of the requests are re-reads the MALL is serving, and that is what sets the
195	time. Blocked, issue falls 4.7x and DRAM reaches **206 GB/s, 87% of the bus**.
196	The GEMM crossover moves out 4x and splits by projection: the `down` tie at
197	t=64 becomes a 1.16x win, and at t=256 `gate_up` stays 1.70x ahead of the GEMM
198	while `down` goes to it, because a 16-row tile covers 5.05 rows in one pass
199	where a compile-time block of 4 needs 1.62. Single-stream decode is unchanged
200	at 5.43 ms and 184 tok/s — this is a throughput lever with no latency effect.
201	
202	The *other* axis of that block is what closed the one cell this suite had left
203	open on the decode path. The `down` projection read **198 GB/s** per distinct
204	expert where `gate_up` read **235**, for the same 845 KB of weights either
205	way; what differs is the aspect ratio, 2560 rows of 640 against 640 rows of
206	2560, so down launches 4x the workgroups and issues 4x the output writes. Two
207	arms that divide the workgroup count *identically* separate the causes:
208	packing several subgroups into a workgroup (`-DROWS=n`, same waves, same
209	loads, same stores) is worth **1.02x**, while giving one subgroup several of
210	an expert's weight rows against one activation row (`-DNROWS=n`, so the wave
211	count falls too) is worth **1.17x** and takes down to **98% of gate_up's
212	rate**. Fitting `T = A/n + B` prices the difference exactly: **19.8% of down's
213	time is a fixed cost per output row** — one `subgroupAdd`, one store, one
214	activation row, paid four times as often against a quarter of the loads — and
215	**-0.4% of gate_up's is**. It is not the lanes, twice over: halving the wave
216	is a wash, and the one build that actually *fills* down's 64 lanes (VEC=1, 80
217	loads per row) is **1.05x slower** than the VEC=4 build whose 44 idle lanes
218	the N block leaves exactly as idle as it found them. The sizing rule is the
219	load-width rule read along the other axis of the matrix — **one lane-step
220	should cover a weight row (`VEC`), and one wave-step should cover the lanes
221	(`NROWS >= 8*VEC*WAVE/K`)** — which is 4 at K=640 and 1 at K=2560, as
222	measured. Unlike the M block this one takes nothing from routing, never pads,
223	and is a **latency** lever: a single token's MoE FFN goes to **5.15 ms over 48
224	layers, 194 tok/s, 97% of its 5.00 ms bus floor**, and `down` beats the Q4
225	grouped GEMM by 1.38x at 64 sequences where the M block managed 1.16x.
226	
227	Those two blocks are the two axes of one kernel, and **putting both in one
228	wave is where a serving batch actually sits**. A workgroup takes `MROWS` of an
229	expert's routed tokens and each of its subgroups takes `NROWS` of that
230	expert's weight rows, so every weight load is dotted `MROWS` times and every
231	activation load `NROWS` times. They **compose**: at 256 sequences in flight it
232	is **1.12x each of its own axes on `gate_up` and 1.19x on `down`**, **1.10x
233	the best single-axis build of any width in the sweep** at both shapes, and
234	1.54x/2.11x the unblocked kernel. At 16-64 tokens it ties the best
235	single-axis build within 1% — those cells are already at the bus — and below
236	that, where the M block is a real loss, the corner loses with it. What that buys is the last of the decode path's
237	bandwidth: `gate_up` reads **228 GB/s of distinct weight bytes, 96% of the
238	bus**, where the M block alone reached 87% and the unblocked kernel 63%, and
239	the FFN runs at **818 tok/s against the Q4 grouped GEMM's 545** — so `down`,
240	which the M block had handed to the GEMM at five rows per expert (0.77x),
241	comes back to **0.98x** there and `gate_up` to 1.88x. Three things fell out of
242	it. An N block makes the M block's **pad slots 4x cheaper on `gate_up` and
243	1.2x on `down`** — a pad costs a per-wave part, which `NROWS` divides, plus a
244	per-output-row part, which it does not, and down's slot is 2560 output rows
245	against gate_up's 640 — so the fitted "block when it removes one group per
246	6-10 pads" becomes one per **45** pads on gate_up and one per 6.5 on down, and
247	the M block may be sized *above* the mean rows per expert where its rows are
248	few. The row block **partly substitutes for the load width**: `NROWS=4` is
249	worth 1.67x at VEC=1 against 1.37x at VEC=4, and `VEC=1` + `NROWS=4` is the
250	fastest single-axis build at gate_up's 256-sequence cell — a width §1.7's rule
251	calls the worst available. And the corner **never spills**: 83 VGPRs at
252	(4, 4) against the plain kernel's 47, with no scratch access anywhere in the
253	family, so the register competition the arm was built to look for does not
254	appear. Single-stream decode is unchanged at 195 tok/s, since the M axis is a
255	loss at one row per expert.
256	
257	The last cell under the bus — `down` at 256 sequences, 66% of it — closed by
258	taking the M block out of the binary. `MROWS` is a compile-time constant and
259	routing is not: at 256 sequences an expert gets 5.05 pairs on average with a
260	tail out to 12, so a compiled block of four spends **23% of its slots on
261	padding**. A two-term cost model (`T = groups*w + slots*s`, fitted from the
262	rows the sweep already produces) reads the width off the routing histogram
263	instead, and it **picks the width that actually won in 28 of 40 cells and is
264	within 1% in 32**, against a 1.11-1.66x spread across the four built widths —
265	and **calibrating it once, at the cheapest batch there is, is as good as
266	re-fitting it per batch**. Then the width stops having to be one number at all:
267	a group's slots must all name one expert, but the width is fixed per
268	*dispatch*, so bucketing the groups by width and issuing one dispatch per
269	bucket covers the histogram with several widths at once, out of the binaries
270	that already exist. On `down` at a serving batch that is worth **1.09-1.13x**
271	over the best fixed width — 2.761 ms to **2.530 ms**, 157 to **169 GB/s** of
272	distinct weight bytes, 66% to **72%** of the bus — and takes a token's MoE FFN
273	at 256 sequences to **848 tok/s** against the Q4 grouped GEMM's 545, with
274	`down` itself back from the GEMM it had gone to (0.99x → **1.07x**), so both
275	projections are the GEMV's at every batch measured.
276	
277	The interesting half is the plan that *loses*. Two ways to cover an expert
278	routed five pairs: one group of eight (three pads, one weight read) or a four
279	and a one (no pads, two weight reads). The pad-minimal plan gets the slot count
280	down to a 5% pad where the fixed build ran 23% — and it is **0.72-0.96x**,
281	losing by up to 1.4x, while the plan that gives each expert a single width
282	repeated wins. What separates them is the one quantity a cost model written in
283	groups and slots cannot see: whether an expert's groups land in the same
284	dispatch. Pricing the residual against a count of the ones that do not gives
285	**3.3-5.9 µs per crossing, against 3.58 µs for a cold DRAM read of that
286	expert's 845 KB**, where a group *inside* the part is priced at 0.45-1.67 µs.
287	So a group is not a fixed cost: one whose expert the previous dispatch just
288	read is a cache hit, and one whose expert was last read a dispatch ago pays the
289	bus again — the same mechanism the M block was buying all along, seen from the
290	side where it can be lost. Barriers between the parts cost +0.2-1.3%, so it is
291	locality and not scheduling. **An expert belongs to exactly one dispatch**, and
292	the fitted "a group is worth 45 pad slots on gate_up, 6.5 on down" turns out to
293	be a *cache-resident* number — at 256 sequences it is 1.0-2.7 on both.
294	What is left of down's deficit is not the table: it is the per-output-row cost
295	inside the wave, paid over four times as many rows, which is the one kernel arm
296	this file has never built.
297	
298	No third-party Go modules — `go.mod` has no dependencies. Vulkan access is a
299	hand-written cgo binding straight against the system Vulkan loader
300	(`vulkan/vulkan.h` + `libvulkan.so`), with the struct-heavy parts of the
301	Vulkan API built in a small C shim (`vk/shim.c`/`vk/shim.h`) rather than Go,
302	since cgo forbids passing a Go struct across the boundary when one of its
303	fields is itself a pointer into other Go memory — and Vulkan's
304	`*CreateInfo` structs are built almost entirely out of such chains.
305	
306	## Layout
307	
308	- `vk/` — the engine: `shim.c`/`shim.h` do the actual Vulkan calls
309	  (instance/device setup with optional fp16/int8/cooperative-matrix/
310	  subgroup-size-control device features, buffer allocation preferring
311	  device-local+host-visible memory, N-buffer pipeline creation with push
312	  constants, specialization constants and an optional required subgroup size,
313	  GPU-timestamp-timed dispatch); `engine.go` is the idiomatic Go wrapper
314	  (`Instance`, `Device`, `Buffer`, `ShaderModule`, `ComputePipeline`).
315	- `main.go` — the original demo: picks the Strix Halo iGPU, uploads a float
316	  array, runs `shaders/double.comp`, reads it back, verifies it.
317	- `shaders/*.comp` — the compute shaders (GLSL); `shaders/shaders.go`
318	  embeds their compiled SPIR-V via `go:embed`. Precision/tile-size variants
319	  of the same source are generated via `glslc -D` flags, not duplicated GLSL.
320	- `cmd/probe/main.go` — dispatches a single `.spv` once, so
321	  `RADV_DEBUG=asm` / `RADV_DEBUG=shaderstats` can be pointed at any shader to
322	  read its disassembly or its VGPR/LDS/spill counts. An optional second
323	  argument pins the wave size the shader is compiled for, since the register
324	  file is per lane and the VGPR count is a different number at each. Note that
325	  RADV caches compiled pipelines, so a repeat probe of the same shader prints
326	  nothing — set `MESA_SHADER_CACHE_DISABLE=1`. Compilation-time questions
327	  only; it binds dummy buffers and computes nothing meaningful.
328	- `bench/` — the benchmark harness: GPU-timestamp-based timing
329	  (`bench.go`), fp16/int8/int4 quantization helpers matching GGML-style
330	  block scales (`quant.go`), clock/power instrumentation (`sysmon.go`), and
331	  one file per op family (`ops_*.go`) wiring shader variants + buffer
332	  layouts + a CPU-reference correctness check to a size sweep.
333	  `modelshapes.go` is the odd one out: not code but data — the weight-matrix
334	  dimensions of the models in `GOALS.md`, with the config each was read from.
335	  `ops_moe.go` is the only family that needs more than one dispatch shape per
336	  measurement: its per-expert baseline is a command buffer of 512 dispatches
337	  with differing push constants, which is `vk.ComputePipeline`'s
338	  `DispatchSequenceTimed`. `ops_moe_q4.go` is its 4-bit arm — the same
339	  routing, tile table and schedules against a Q4 expert bank, so the two
340	  formats' rows subtract. `ops_moe_gemv.go` is the decode kernel and its two
341	  compile-time blocks, and `ops_moe_select.go` is what replaces them with a
342	  choice: a cost model fitted from those rows, a plan that covers the routing
343	  histogram with several block widths at once, and `vk.DispatchMultiTimed` —
344	  the one timed sequence in the harness whose dispatches differ in their
345	  *pipeline* rather than just their push constants.
346	- `cmd/bench/main.go` — the benchmark CLI; `bench/families.go` is the
347	  registry of targetable op families it dispatches to.
348	- `results/` — one CSV per op family, the committed measurements.
349

351	
352	- Go, gcc/clang, `pkg-config`
353	- Vulkan loader + headers (`vulkan-icd-loader`, `vulkan-headers` on Arch)
354	- `glslc` (from `shaderc`) to compile shaders — only needed when a `.comp`

357	## Usage
358	
359	```sh
360	go generate ./...   # only needed after editing a .comp file
361	go build ./...
362	
363	./strix-halo-vulkan   # original demo
364	
365	go run ./cmd/bench -list          # the op families a run can target
366	go run ./cmd/bench gemv gemv_cold # run two of them
367	go run ./cmd/bench all            # the whole suite (~60 min)
368	                                  # -h for the sweep flags (sizes, blocks,
369	                                  # warmup/iters, per-family sweeps)
370	```
371	
372	A run has to name what it is measuring: the full suite takes well over half
373	an hour and produces ~2600 rows, so sweeping all of it to answer one question is
374	mostly waste. `all` is still there for the occasions that want it.
375	
376	`cmd/bench` prints a results table per op family and writes one CSV per
377	family into `-resultsdir` (default `results/`) — `results/gemv.csv`,
378	`results/stride.csv`, and so on. Each file is written as soon as its family
379	finishes, so an interrupted run keeps what completed, and re-running one
380	family refreshes only its own file and leaves the rest of the committed
381	numbers untouched. Every file has the same columns:
382	`op,variant,weight_format,block_size,size,ns_per_iter,gflops,gbps` followed
383	by `sclk_mhz,sclk_mhz_min,sclk_mhz_max,power_w,detail`, so
384	`tail -q -n +2 results/*.csv` reconstructs the single flat table the suite
385	used to write if an analysis wants it.
386	
387	The families are the twelve listed by `-list`: `peak`, `overhead`,
388	`bandwidth`, `stride`, `elementwise`, `gemv`, `gemv_cold`, `gemm`,
389	`gemm_wmma`, `shapes`, `moe`, `reduce`. `gemm_wmma` — the hand-tuned WMMA
390	ladder — is separate from `gemm` because it is the larger half of the GEMM
391	rows and is iterated on by itself. `shapes` and `moe` are the two that sweep
392	nothing: `shapes` runs the kernels the other families picked over the real
393	model dimensions in `bench/modelshapes.go` (~5 min), and `moe` runs the
394	grouped/MoE GEMM over qwen3.8-flash-next's 512-expert bank at fp16 and at
395	4 bits, plus the grouped W4A8 GEMV the decode half of that block wants
396	(~18 min). Both ignore `-sizes`/`-blocks`, because their shapes are the
397	models' rather than the flags'. `moe` also allocates the largest buffers in
398	the suite — a 512-expert fp16 weight bank is 1.8-4.0 GB depending on the row
399	stride under test — so it wants headroom rather than a loaded machine; its Q4
400	GEMM arm runs in a second pass once those are freed and its GEMV arm in a
401	third, so no two banks are ever live at the same time.
402	
403	## Reading the numbers honestly
404	
405	Four op families exist to keep the rest of the suite interpretable. They
406	are cheap to run and worth running first.
407	
408	- **`peak`** measures the hardware's instruction-issue ceilings with kernels
409	  whose operands are register-resident before the loop, so nothing in the
410	  timed loop touches memory (`shaders/alu_peak.comp`): scalar fp32 FMA,
411	  packed-fp16 FMA, `dotPacked4x8` (int8 packed dot), and cooperative-matrix
412	  fp16 and int8. Every other kernel's GFLOP/s should be read as a fraction
413	  of the relevant one of these — not of a spec-sheet figure extrapolated
414	  from a different chip. `-cus` (default 40) expresses each ceiling as
415	  ops/clock/CU, the form comparable against published RDNA3 figures.
416	- **`overhead`** measures a shader that does nothing, isolating the cost of
417	  a dispatch plus the pipeline barrier between iterations from any real
418	  work. It bounds how much a long chain of small kernels (decode) can lose
419	  to launch cost, and explains bandwidth measurements at sizes small enough
420	  to be dominated by a fixed cost.
421	- **`stride`** measures what the memory system delivers for a *fixed* set of
422	  bytes as the row stride and the request shape vary — the qualifier on
423	  `bandwidth`, which only ever measures a contiguous sweep and therefore
424	  reports best-case ceilings a strided kernel does not automatically get. One
425	  kernel (`shaders/strided_read.comp`) reads every touched 16-byte chunk
426	  exactly once in every variant, so the byte set and the load count are
427	  identical and only the stride and the lane→address mapping change;
428	  `LANES_PER_ROW` sets how many consecutive chunks of a row go to
429	  consecutive lanes, so one request spans 1 row (contiguous) up to 64 rows (a
430	  gather); `CROSS_WAVE` swaps the traversal so consecutive *requests* advance
431	  down the rows rather than along one, which is the only way to put
432	  concurrent waves a stride apart; and `LOADS_PER_WAVE` gives each request
433	  more of its row in flight, up to a whole row, which is what a real kernel's
434	  inner loop does. `-stridepads`, `-striderowbytes` and `-stridefootprints`
435	  set the three sweeps; the printed grid carries a `model` row giving
436	  `min(1, C/gcd(stride, 4096))`, and the cross-wave grid under it carries the
437	  same model per shape, which the measurements track to within 2% wherever C
438	  is a genuine contiguous run and only indicatively for the gather shapes. Each case is checked against a host checksum
439	  over its (row, chunk) set, so a mis-derived index fails instead of
440	  reporting a plausible bandwidth — and the shapes where both traversals
441	  compile to the same mapping are marked, since those cells measure
442	  repeatability rather than traversal.
443	- **`gemv_cold`** measures the decode-shape GEMV against weights several
444	  times larger than the last-level cache. The square `gemv` sweep's largest
445	  case holds 33.5MB of fp16 weights (16.8MB at int8, 8.4MB at int4), which
446	  fits this chip's ~32MB MALL, and then re-reads it hundreds of times — so
447	  it reports bandwidth above what the DRAM bus can deliver and flatters the
448	  formats that read *more* bytes, since cached bytes are nearly free. Real
449	  decode streams a whole model from DRAM per token. `-coldfootprints` sets
450	  the swept weight footprints in MB (fp16-equivalent, so every format in a
451	  row holds the same number of weights), `-coldn` the reduction length.
452	- **`shapes`** is the check on everything above: the same kernels, at the
453	  dimensions the models in `GOALS.md` are actually made of, because a square
454	  N x N x N sweep ties three independent variables together and every real
455	  layer separates them. Its decode arm gives each reduction length a
456	  DRAM-resident twin — the model's own row geometry, with enough rows that
457	  the weights cannot fit the MALL — because a single real weight matrix is
458	  usually small enough to be cache-resident on its own while the model it
459	  belongs to is not. Its prefill arm pads M and N up to the kernel's tile and
460	  charges the padding to the result: the reported GFLOP/s is the model's own
461	  FLOPs over the padded dispatch's time, so a 40-row expert in a 64-row tile
462	  reads as the 62%-efficient thing it is, with the rate the kernel itself hit
463	  in `exec_gflops`. K is never padded — that would compute a different
464	  product — so a variant whose K-slab does not divide the model's K is
465	  skipped instead. The arm runs a 200-iteration floor rather than the suite's
466	  20: these dispatches are tens of microseconds, and at 20 iterations a few
467	  cells per run came back 2x low at a pinned clock.
468	
469	Three measurement hazards the harness handles rather than leaves to the
470	reader:
471	
472	- **Clock.** This GPU idles at 637 MHz out of 2900 (see
473	  `/sys/class/drm/cardN/device/pp_dpm_sclk`), and host-side work between
474	  cases — generating and quantizing hundreds of MB of weights — lets it
475	  drop back. Before each timed measurement the harness drives the GPU with
476	  ALU-heavy work until the clock reaches 97% of its advertised maximum
477	  (`-warmclock` bounds how long it will try; it stops as soon as the target
478	  is reached, so a hot GPU costs one 20ms burst), and records the clock and
479	  power actually observed during the measurement in every result row. An
480	  earlier sweep without this reported the same kernel at 190 GFLOP/s and
481	  522 GFLOP/s depending only on how long the preceding case had kept the
482	  CPU busy.
483	- **GPU-hang watchdog.** `bench.TimeDispatch` probes each case with one
484	  dispatch before batching more into a single timed submission, capping the
485	  batch so it can't run long enough to trip the kernel driver's GPU-hang
486	  timeout (amdgpu's default TDR is commonly ~10s) — a slow kernel (e.g.
487	  naive GEMM at large sizes) is simply measured with fewer iterations
488	  rather than risking `VK_ERROR_DEVICE_LOST`, which would otherwise poison
489	  the device for every case still queued.
490	- **Operand stride.** A sweep over powers of two sweeps, by construction,
491	  only the strides that alias worst on this memory system. Two distinct
492	  things go wrong there (IDEAS §2.3, §5.1b): a load whose addresses are all
493	  one stride apart aims them at a single 256 B-interleaved channel when that
494	  stride is a multiple of the 4 KB interleave rotation, costing up to 1.34x
495	  of bandwidth and up to 1.6x on a WMMA GEMM; and — the larger one —
496	  whenever the bytes the concurrent waves hold in flight cover less of the
497	  4 KB rotation than `gcd(stride, 4096)`, the remaining channels are never
498	  addressed at all, costing 2x, 4x or 8x even for a contiguous read and even
499	  with no padding present. The `gemm` family's WMMA cases therefore take
500	  both leading dimensions as push constants and carry `strideA`/`strideB` in
501	  their `detail` column, and the `_pada128`/`_pad*` rows are the same SPIR-V
502	  at a padded stride — so a row's stride is visible rather than implied by
503	  its size. Nothing outside that family has been measured against a padded
504	  stride yet; assume its numbers are the aliased ones.
505	- **Wave size.** Every kernel whose workgroup *is* one subgroup takes `WAVE`
506	  as a `glslc -D`, and the pipeline pins the matching size with
507	  `VK_EXT_subgroup_size_control`'s `requiredSubgroupSize`
508	  (`PipelineSpec.RequiredSubgroupSize`) — the two must agree or a 32-thread
509	  binary would run as a half-idle wave64 and `subgroupAdd` would reduce half a
510	  row. The `*_w32` rows are those pairs; they are dropped whole, with a note on
511	  stderr, on a device that will not let a pipeline name a size. It is not a
512	  free knob in either direction: up to 2.1x on a fragment-heavy WMMA tile, and
513	  0.58-0.9x almost everywhere else (IDEAS §6.2). The 1.07x it used to be worth
514	  on the DRAM-resident W4A8 decode GEMV was not a wave-size effect at all —
515	  at equal bytes-of-row-per-lane-step the two sizes measure the same to 0.05%
516	  (IDEAS §1.7). Rows without `_w32` are at the driver's default of 64.
517	- **W4A8 load width (`VEC`) and rows per workgroup (`ROWS`).**
518	  `gemv_w4a8.comp` takes both as `glslc -D`s: `VEC` ∈ {1,4,8,16} is `uvec4`s
519	  of weights per lane per step (`subgroup`, `_vec4`, `_vec8`, `_vec16` rows),
520	  `ROWS` is subgroups per workgroup (`_r2`). `VEC` is the one that matters and
521	  its right value depends on the reduction length — `N/(8·WAVE)`, so a row is
522	  covered in one step — which is why the rows are swept rather than one
523	  variant kept. `ROWS` changes nothing anywhere except the single cell where
524	  `VEC` is one step short of a row, and is kept as the control that showed
525	  that (IDEAS §1.7).
526	- **The grouped arm's two blocks (`MROWS`, `NROWS`).** `gemv_w4a8.comp
527	  -DGROUPED=1 -DMROWS=m -DNROWS=n` gives one workgroup *m* routed tokens of
528	  the same expert and each of its subgroups *n* of that expert's weight rows
529	  (`_m2`, `_n4`, `_m4_n4` rows). They combine, and they are sized by different
530	  things. `NROWS` is a model constant like `VEC` — `8*VEC*WAVE/K`, so 4 at
531	  K=640 and 1 at K=2560 — and never hurts at the shapes it is sized for.
532	  `MROWS` has to match how many rows routing gives an expert and is a real
533	  loss when it does not (0.39x at one row per expert, 1.66x at five), so an
534	  engine keeps several builds and picks per dispatch. Both require `GROUPED`;
535	  `NROWS` is capped at 4 when combined with an M block, and `ROWS` (subgroups
536	  per workgroup) works under `GROUPED` too, as the control that showed the
537	  cost is inside the wave rather than in the grid (IDEAS §1.9, §1.10, §1.11).
538	- **Cache-resident measurements are contended.** A MALL-resident working
539	  set is shared with everything else touching memory — the display this iGPU
540	  also drives, or a second benchmark process — and losing part of it drops a
541	  case towards DRAM speed. With another benchmark running alongside, one in
542	  ten MALL-resident `stride` cases lands at 0.3-0.5x, on a different cell
543	  each run, with sclk and fclk both pinned; with sole use of the GPU the
544	  large dropouts vanish and ~10% one-sided scatter remains. Contention can
545	  only make a case slower, so that family runs each case three times and
546	  keeps the fastest. DRAM-resident cases reproduce to within 2% and are
547	  unaffected. Run one benchmark at a time, and treat cache-resident numbers
548	  elsewhere in the suite as carrying the same one-sided noise.
549	- **The first cache-resident case after a host fill is not a measurement.**
550	  Filling a 128 MiB buffer from the CPU cost the next case 13-17%,
551	  reproducibly by *position* rather than by access pattern: it came out at
552	  exactly 782 GB/s in all three row-length groups of one run, while a
553	  shape-identical twin measured immediately afterwards read 942 and the
554	  clock differed by 1%. `RunStride` now runs and discards one case per
555	  group, which puts those cells back at 884-950. Writeback from the fill
556	  competing for DRAM is the likeliest cause; it was never visible in the
557	  DRAM-resident groups.
558	
559	## Adding a new shader
560	
561	1. Write `shaders/foo.comp`.
562	2. Add a `//go:generate glslc ... -o foo.spv foo.comp` line and a
563	   `//go:embed foo.spv` var in `shaders/shaders.go`.
564	3. Run `go generate ./...`.
565	4. Build a pipeline for it via `Device.NewPipeline(shader, vk.PipelineSpec{...})`
566	   in `vk/engine.go` — it takes any number of storage-buffer bindings, an
567	   optional push-constant size, and optional specialization constants.
568	5. To benchmark it, add a `bench/ops_*.go` case following the existing
569	   ones: build buffers/pipeline, run one untimed dispatch and compare
570	   against a CPU reference before trusting any timing, then call
571	   `bench.TimeDispatch`. Verify once at a small fixed size, never inside
572	   the size sweep — an O(N³) CPU reference GEMM at N=4096 is ~137 billion
573	   scalar operations in pure Go.
574
